collection.title: Which Attention Helps? A Slide-Level Ablation of Attention-Augmented CNNs for Serous Ovarian Carcinoma Grading
collection.abstract:
BackgroundDistinguishing high-grade (HGSC) from low-grade serous carcinoma (LGSC) is clinically consequential yet difficult, as the subtypes share a serous morphology but differ in prognosis and treatment. Prior deep-learning studies report near-perfect accuracy, but often under patch-level evaluation that leaks slide information between training and testing.

MethodsWe present a leakage-controlled, slide-level ablation of attention-augmented CNNs for this binary task on the UBC-OCEAN cohort (259 whole-slide images; 217 HGSC, 42 LGSC). Under an identical protocol with five-fold slide-grouped cross-validation, Macenko stain normalisation, and slide-level pooling, we compared a from-scratch backbone with no attention, Squeeze-and-Excitation, channel-only CBAM and full CBAM, a lightweight CBAM variant, and an ImageNet-pretrained MobileNet with a differential-attention module. A pathology foundation model (Phikon) with attention-based multiple-instance aggregation was evaluated as a modern benchmark. Results are reported across three training seeds, with decision thresholds selected within folds, and compared using DeLong and McNemar tests with Holm correction and bootstrap confidence intervals.

ResultsThe pretrained model performed best (AUC 0.862 {+/-} 0.005, MCC 0.460) and was the most stable across seeds. It significantly outranked both the Squeeze-and-Excitation model (DeLong, Holm p = 0.002) and the no-attention baseline (p = 0.019). Full CBAM also outranked Squeeze-and-Excitation (p = 0.010), but adding the spatial-attention branch to channel attention produced no detectable change (0.824 to 0.822; p = 0.50), and the lightweight model did not match the deep one once training variance was accounted for. The foundation-model benchmark reached AUC 0.834 {+/-} 0.018, below the pretrained MobileNet. A colour-only classifier reached AUC 0.66, indicating part of the separability is attributable to stain and colour rather than morphology.

ConclusionUnder leakage-free evaluation, performance is more modest than commonly reported. Transfer learning and the avoidance of a weak channel-only configuration produced the clearest gains, while finer attention design, network size and a pathology-specific foundation model produced no detectable improvement. With only 42 LGSC slides the task remains underpowered for finer distinctions, and most architectural differences could not be resolved.

collection.title: Reference calibration, autozygosity and blood-derived variant interpretation in older adults
collection.authors: El-Haddad, M.; Hendi, N.; El-Hajj Fuleihan, G.; Nemer, G.; El-Hachem, N.
collection.abstract:
Population exomes contain signals of demographic history, inherited disease alleles and, when derived from blood, possible acquired variation. Distinguishing these signals is important in underrepresented populations, where reference absence can reflect both sampling and local frequency differences. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first Levantine old-age cohort characterized by whole exomes. We reanalyzed blood-derived exomes from 199 Lebanese trial participants aged 65-91 years, including 187 unrelated participants for frequency and recessive analyses. Twenty-nine participants (14.6%) reached the autozygosity expected for offspring of first cousins. Although 13.8% of observed autosomal alleles were absent at callable gnomAD Middle Eastern reference sites, size matching gave a reference-to-cohort single-nucleotide variant absence ratio of 0.98. Excess absence was concentrated among recurrent alleles; 360 were absent from the full reference, none classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar. Separately, regional disease alleles showed nominal frequency differences, including MEFV p.Val726Ala (0.051 versus 0.012). Qualifying recessive alleles occurred in 55.1% of unrelated participants, decreasing to 45.5% after severity-related exclusions. Conditional qualifying biallelic genotype estimates increased from 2.0 to 27.7 per 1,000 offspring between unrelated-parent and first-cousin inbreeding coefficients. Twelve participants had clonal-driver candidates, but only five met both binomial and empirical allele-fraction criteria for the probable tier; a TP53 frameshift remained unresolved. Eight participants (4.0%) had unconfirmed, condition-matched candidate secondary findings. These observations distinguish reference sampling from allele-specific frequency differences and genotype expectations from clinical outcomes. They support complementary checks on population exome interpretation, while leaving generalizability, variant origin and clinical reportability to independent evaluation.

Author SummaryWe studied genetic variation in 199 older adults from Lebanon to understand how population differences and aging can complicate the interpretation of genetic tests. A change missing from a reference database might be locally common, but it might also be missing simply because the database sampled too few people. We compared equally sized samples and found that the overall absence of observed changes was similar in the regional reference and another part of our study group. Individual disease-associated changes could nevertheless have different local frequencies. We also examined stretches of DNA inherited from shared ancestors and estimated how parental relatedness could change the chance of pairing disease-associated copies. These estimates describe genetic combinations, not predicted numbers of affected children. Finally, because blood cells can acquire changes during aging, we compared candidate changes with the sequencing patterns of other variants in the same data. Some findings remained uncertain, and none was clinically confirmed. Our results show why reference sampling, shared ancestry and possible acquired changes need separate consideration before drawing conclusions about inherited risk.

collection.title: Evaluating the Incremental Value of AI-Derived ECG Features Beyond Automated ECG Reports and Clinical Data for 30-Day Mortality: A MIMIC-IV Cohort Study
collection.authors: Park, S.-H.; Ji, Z.; Lewey, J.; Tsui, F.
collection.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) reports and clinical records already carry prognostic information, so the relevant question is what artificial intelligence (AI)-derived ECG waveform features add beyond these existing sources, and whether models with similar overall discrimination would prioritize the same patients for review. In linked Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) data, we compared 15 prespecified ECG morphology measurements with features from a previously trained deep-learning model for 30-day all-cause mortality in the same 25,430 held-out patients (924 deaths). Both feature sets fed identical prediction models developed and evaluated with the same procedures; paired 95% confidence intervals quantify each difference, basic clinical history -- age, recorded sex, and prior-diagnosis indicators -- was held constant where indicated, and analyses are labelled prespecified or post hoc. The AI-feature model ranked 30-day mortality risk better than the morphology model (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.812 versus 0.737; +0.075, 95% CI +0.059 to +0.091), and the advantage persisted with basic clinical history (+0.053, +0.039 to +0.067). In post hoc comparisons with basic clinical history held constant, replacing the expanded automated report associated with the index ECG with AI features changed discrimination little (+0.0037, -0.0053 to +0.0126), and adding AI features to the report-based model yielded +0.0075 (-0.0005 to +0.0151); both intervals include zero. At a hypothetical fixed 5% review capacity, the prespecified ECG-only comparison identified 236 versus 163 subsequent deaths (AI features versus morphology measurements), and with basic clinical history the corresponding post hoc comparison identified 262 versus 221. In a separate post hoc comparison using separately refitted models, the AI-feature and expanded-report review lists captured 262 versus 261 subsequent deaths (paired difference +1, 95% CI -25 to +22), yet shared only 654 of their 1,272 flagged patients: similar totals, different patient lists. One-year transport to a Brazilian cohort absent from the models earlier training retained the advantage over morphology measurements. These retrospective risk rankings measure prioritization, not prevented mortality: the advantage over richer routine reports was small and uncertain, and equal-capacity lists flagged different patients, so comparator strength and patient selection merit evaluation alongside discrimination before clinical use.

collection.title: Algorithmic design choices as determinants of health equity: a causal simulation study of healthcare resource allocation
collection.abstract:
BackgroundCare management programs increasingly rely on prediction algorithms to decide which patients receive limited healthcare resources. Because these algorithms are typically trained to predict future healthcare utilization or cost, they may systematically underidentify patients whose care-seeking behavior is suppressed by structural barriers.

ObjectiveTo evaluate how three modifiable design choices (selection threshold, feature set, and training objective) affect allocation equity in care management targeting.

MethodsWe constructed an analytical cohort of 201,216 adults from linked electronic health record and participant survey data in the NIH All of Us Research Program (2017-2019). Three prediction models (logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost) were trained and evaluated under simulation conditions that varied one design choice at a time while holding the others fixed. Equity was assessed using false negative rate (FNR), equal opportunity difference (EOD), and allocation rate conditional on need (an access-independent benchmark based on self-reported general health status). We also applied Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to identify which predictors contributed most to the Black-White allocation gap.

ResultsPrior utilization understated self-reported health burden among disadvantaged groups: 33% of Black and 32% of Hispanic participants reported fair or poor health, yet only 22% and 19% were classified as high utilizers. White participants showed the opposite pattern: 25% were classified as high utilizers, while only 19% reported fair or poor general health status. Under baseline design choices, all three models produced similar disparities, with uninsured participants showing the largest gap (EOD: -0.148). Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition identified prior outpatient visits as the dominant contributor to the Black-White gap in predicted allocation, with higher average emergency department utilization among Black participants partially offsetting the effect. Varying the selection threshold had little effect; disparities persisted across all thresholds. Feature set variation produced mixed and group-specific effects; removal of prior outpatient visits achieved near-zero Black-White EOD (0.001, AUC: 0.77), consistent with the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition finding. Training objective variation produced the most substantial and consistent equity effects, with the health status objective achieving near-zero Black-White EOD (0.008, AUC: 0.69) and the survey-enriched health status condition reversing the direction of disparity for most groups.

ConclusionsAlgorithmic equity in care management targeting is largely a consequence of modifiable design choices, with training objective emerging as the most impactful of the three design choices evaluated. The causal simulation framework and access-independent equity benchmark developed here provide a replicable approach for evaluating equity as a design consideration during algorithm development rather than a post-deployment correction.
